question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old woman with a nine-year history of biopsy-proven cirrhosis attributed to long-standing nonalcoholic steatohepatitis was seen in the early afternoon in the liver disease rapid-access clinic at the request of her endocrinologist after routine surveillance laboratory work drawn last week revealed a rising bilirubin level; the patient herself reported only mild fatigue during evening meal preparation and a tendency for her palms to flush when she took a hot shower, but she denied pruritus, yellowing noticed by coworkers, abdominal swelling, early satiety, ankle puffiness, nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, black or bloody stools, light-headedness, insomnia, personality change, forgetfulness, handwriting alteration, unsteady gait, falls, or tremor. She had never required hospital admission for gastrointestinal bleeding or peritoneal fluid drainage, had not experienced confusion or sleep-wake inversion, and had never been prescribed lactulose, rifaximin, or diuretics. Comorbid conditions include well-controlled type 2 diabetes treated with dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly and metformin 1000 mg twice daily, hypertension managed with amlodipine 5 mg each morning, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine around 0.9 mg/dL. She does not drink alcohol, never smoked, and denies any illicit drug use. Home medications also include low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily, and a prenatal multivitamin she continued after her last pregnancy; she takes no herbal or over-the-counter weight-loss preparations and has no medication allergies. Obstetric history is G2P2, both births uncomplicated; surgical history is limited to laparoscopic cholecystectomy fifteen years prior. Her father died from myocardial infarction at 72, her mother has osteoarthritis, and there is no family history of liver disease. She works as a high-school math teacher, walks two kilometers most mornings, and follows a low-sodium Mediterranean eating pattern taught by a dietitian. Review of systems was otherwise negative for fevers, chills, chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, palpitations, urinary changes, or rash. She arrived by private vehicle and had taken only her usual morning medications; no intravenous fluids, vitamins, or anticoagulants were administered before clinic evaluation. At triage—prior to any phlebotomy or imaging—oral temperature was 36.7 °C, blood pressure 122/72 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. She was alert, conversed briskly, named the hospital and date correctly, counted backward from 100 by sevens without hesitation, recalled three objects at five minutes, copied intersecting pentagons accurately, and maintained outstretched arms with wrists dorsiflexed for thirty seconds without asterixis or tremor. Pupils were equal and reactive, speech clear, cranial nerves II–XII intact, motor strength 5/5 diffusely, sensation intact, reflexes symmetric, and gait down the corridor normal in speed and arm swing. Sclerae displayed a faint golden hue in bright light, conjunctivae were pink, and mild palmar erythema was present; fewer than ten spider angiomas dotted the upper chest. Neck veins were 6 cm H₂O with the head of the exam table at 30°, carotid upstrokes brisk, and the cardiac examination revealed a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lung fields were clear to auscultation with good air entry. The abdominal wall was flat in the supine position with the umbilicus indented; there was no visible bulging of the flanks. Percussion produced tympany throughout without a flank crescent of dullness, and no fluid wave was elicited even when an assistant’s hand was positioned at the midline. The liver edge, firm and finely nodular, was felt 1 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration and was non-tender; the spleen tip was not palpable. There was no pedal edema, ecchymosis, or muscle wasting. Capillary blood glucose measured 106 mg/dL. Immediately afterward—still before any vitamin K, albumin infusion, diuretics, or antibiotics—venous blood was drawn, yielding: total bilirubin 2.56 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.41 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 47 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 63 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 134 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 188 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.4 ×10⁹/L, platelet count 122 ×10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.26. Urinalysis from a clean-catch specimen showed trace bilirubin, moderate urobilinogen, and no protein or infection. A focused abdominal ultrasound performed at the bedside minutes later—prior to any intervention—demonstrated a shrunken heterogeneous liver with capsular nodularity, a patent main portal vein with hepatopetal flow at 17 cm/s, spleen length 15.8 cm, and no free intraperitoneal fluid; kidneys appeared normal in size and echogenicity, and no biliary ductal dilation or focal hepatic mass was identified. Upright posteroanterior chest radiography taken immediately after ultrasound revealed elevated hemidiaphragms but no pleural effusion or infiltrate, and a twelve-lead electrocardiogram recorded normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min with a QTc of 412 ms. At this point in the visit the patient had received no pharmacologic or procedural therapy, so all clinical observations and laboratory values above represent her untreated physiologic state at presentation for evaluation of mildly worsening jaundice in the context of established nonalcoholic steatohepatitis–related cirrhosis.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Child-Pugh grades five findings from 1 to 3 points each. Use the pretreatment findings and the standard bilirubin thresholds for NASH cirrhosis:
- Total bilirubin (<2, 2–3, >3 mg/dL): 2.56 mg/dL → 2.
- Albumin (>3.5, 2.8–3.5, <2.8 g/dL): 3.41 g/dL → 2.
- INR (<1.7, 1.7–2.3, >2.3): 1.26 → 1.
- Ascites (absent, mild/controlled, moderate-to-severe despite treatment): none on examination or ultrasound → 1.
- Hepatic encephalopathy (absent, grade I–II, grade III–IV): intact cognition without confusion or asterixis → 1.
Total = 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 7 (Child-Pugh class B).
Final answer: 7
